raw_case_text:
Written informed consent was taken from the patient for the publication of this report and accompanying images. A 66-year-old man was diagnosed as having FL, grade2, Stage IVB according to the Ann Arbor disease staging system. He had received hormone replacement therapy with 15 mg of hydrocortisone for primary hypogonadism for 11 years before the diagnosis of FL. After the first-line therapy of six cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone) therapy, he achieved complete response (CR) and was subjected to rituximab maintenance therapy. However, 6 months after achievement of the first CR, the disease relapsed with the emergence of systemic lymph node swelling and skin involvement on his left shoulder, without the evidence of histologic transformation. Salvage therapy with five cycles of CHASER therapy (cyclophosphamide, high-dose cytarabine, dexamethasone, etoposide, and rituximab) successfully induced a second CR. Although the consolidative high-dose chemotherapy supported by autologous HSCT with rituximab in vivo purging was initially planned for the relapsed FL in this patient, this attempt was not accomplished due to mobilization failure of hematopoietic stem cells, and the patient was subjected to watchful observation without treatment. The patient developed CMV retinitis 3 months later, and since then, the patient repeatedly developed CMV antigenemia and retinitis, despite appropriate treatment with valacyclovir. Substitution therapy with intravenous immunoglobulins was also administered every 4 weeks for secondary hypogammaglobulinemia to maintain the serum immunoglobulin G level over 500 mg/dL.
Eighteen months after completion of CHASER therapy, at the age of 68 years, the patient was hospitalized with the chief complaints of pyrexia, cough, and hypoxemia. Upon admission, blood tests revealed a normal leukocyte count of 6.30x109/L (normal range: 3.30-8.60x109/L) comprising 3.83x109/L neutrophils (1.24-4.61x109/L), 0.49x109/L CD4-positive T cells (0.37-1.44x109/L), 2.44x109/L CD8-positive T cells (0.26-1.16x109/L), with a CD4:CD8 ratio=0.2, and 1.29x109/L B cells (0.10-0.46x109/L). Mild anemia of 11.2 g/dL (13.7-16.8 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia of 112.0x109/L (158-348x109/L) were present. Serological tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein of 14.92 mg/dL (0.00-0.30 mg/dL), while lactate dehydrogenase (257 IU/L [120-240 IU/L]) and KL-6 (206 U/mL [<500 U/mL]) were within the normal range. Serum immunoglobulin G level was maintained at 873 mg/dL by intravenous immunoglobulins. Serum immunoglobulin A and M levels were 234 mg/dL (102-411 mg/dL) and 176 mg/dL (30-207 mg/dL), respectively. Although the chest X-ray did not show major abnormal shadows (Figure 1), computed tomography (CT) images identified nodular abnormal shadows in both lungs without lymphoma relapse, revealing that the patient was complicated by pulmonary infection (Figure 2A, B). In the absence of positive bacterial/fungal culture tests or positive serological/blood tests for Aspergillus antigen, Candida albicans antigen, Mycoplasma antibody, beta-d-glucan, and CMV-pp65 antigen, the patient received empiric antibiotic treatments, including piperacillin/tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, and liposomal amphotericin B. However, the pneumonia got worse, as shown by chest CT images on the 10th day of treatment (Figure 2C, D). Thirteen days after admission, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests were performed for herpes simplex virus type 1, herpes simplex virus type 2, varicella-zoster virus, CMV, parvovirus B19, BK virus, John Cunningham virus, Epstein-Barr virus, HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8, and hepatitis B virus on a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) sample. As the result, only HHV-6 DNA was detected by PCR in the BAL fluid, while HHV-6 DNA was not detected in plasma on the same day as the BAL examination. In addition, no bacterium or fungus was detected as pathogens in the BAL fluid. He was diagnosed as having HHV-6 pneumonitis, and intravenous ganciclovir (GCV; 5 mg/kg, q12h) therapy was initiated from day14, which quickly resolved the fever and cough within a couple of days and improved the CT findings by day 21 (Figure 2E, F). GCV treatment was changed to oral valganciclovir treatment on day 22, which was discontinued on day 40. Since then, no recurrence of HHV-6 pneumonitis has been observed for more than a year. During the course, the patient showed no symptoms of other HHV-6-associated end-organ damage.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old man with relapsed stage IVB follicular lymphoma in second complete remission presented with fever, cough, and hypoxemia 18 months after salvage CHASER chemoimmunotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed at age 66 with stage IVB grade 2 follicular lymphoma, the patient achieved first CR after 6 cycles of R-CHOP + rituximab maintenance, relapsed at 6 months, and achieved second CR after 5 cycles of salvage CHASER therapy (with failed autologous stem cell mobilization). Three months post-CHASER, he developed recurrent CMV antigenemia and CMV retinitis managed with valacyclovir and monthly IVIG for secondary hypogammaglobulinemia. Eighteen months post-CHASER (at age 68), he presented with fever, cough, and hypoxemia, with bilateral nodular lung infiltrates that worsened over 10 days despite empirical piperacillin/tazobactam, ciprofloxacin, voriconazole, and liposomal amphotericin B.
subjective.past_medical_history: Relapsed stage IVB grade 2 follicular lymphoma status post R-CHOP (6 cycles), rituximab maintenance, and salvage CHASER chemoimmunotherapy (5 cycles); secondary hypogammaglobulinemia on monthly IVIG; recurrent CMV antigenemia and CMV retinitis on valacyclovir; primary hypogonadism on hydrocortisone replacement (15 mg/day) for 11 years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, cough, and hypoxemia; negative for extrapulmonary HHV-6 end-organ symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Presented with pyrexia, cough, and hypoxemia.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed normal WBC count of 6.30 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 3.83 x 10^9/L, CD4+ T cells 0.49 x 10^9/L, CD8+ T cells 2.44 x 10^9/L [CD4:CD8 ratio 0.2], B cells 1.29 x 10^9/L), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (platelets 112.0 x 10^9/L), elevated CRP (14.92 mg/dL), mildly elevated LDH (257 IU/L), normal KL-6 (206 U/mL), IgG 873 mg/dL (on IVIG), IgA 234 mg/dL, and IgM 176 mg/dL. Admission chest X-ray showed no major abnormalities.
objective.advanced_workup: Admission chest CT demonstrated bilateral nodular pulmonary opacities without lymphoma relapse, which progressed on day 10 chest CT despite broad-spectrum antibacterial and antifungal therapy. Blood/serological tests for Aspergillus antigen, Candida albicans antigen, beta-D-glucan, Mycoplasma antibody, and CMV pp65 antigen were all negative. On hospital day 13, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) viral multiplex PCR panel (testing HSV-1/2, VZV, CMV, parvovirus B19, BKV, JCV, EBV, HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8, and HBV) was positive exclusively for human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) DNA in BAL fluid (with negative plasma HHV-6 DNA and negative BAL bacterial and fungal cultures).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Primary pulmonary human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) pneumonitis in an immunocompromised follicular lymphoma patient with inverted CD4:CD8 ratio and hypogammaglobulinemia; invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, candidiasis, and CMV pneumonitis were ruled out by negative serum Aspergillus and Candida antigens, negative beta-D-glucan, negative BAL fungal/bacterial cultures, and lack of response to voriconazole and liposomal amphotericin B, while HHV-6 pneumonitis was confirmed by selective HHV-6 DNA detection in BAL fluid. Initiated intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg q12h) on hospital day 14, achieving rapid resolution of fever and cough within 2 days and marked chest CT improvement by day 21, followed by oral valganciclovir (days 22-40) with no recurrence over >1 year of follow-up.
